blocks.text: A typical path from application data to hardware can include a file, filesystem, logical volume, partition, block device, storage controller, and physical media. Not every system uses every layer. A filesystem can live directly on a block device, and cloud or virtual storage adds layers outside the guest.
Each layer has its own identity, size, and failure modes. A larger disk does not automatically enlarge its filesystem. A healthy filesystem does not prove the physical storage is reliable.

Draw the actual stack before changing it. Use findmnt, lsblk, and, where applicable, LVM tools. Record which layer owns the change requested by the application team. The correct command follows from that model, not from the phrase “add space.”
Linux example — 9.1
Observe disks, partitions, and mounts together.

lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
findmnt

blocks.text: A block device exposes addressable storage blocks. Linux paths can include /dev/sda, /dev/vda, or /dev/nvme0n1, depending on the device and driver. Partition names follow device-specific conventions, such as /dev/nvme0n1p1.
These short names can change when hardware discovery order changes. Persistent paths under /dev/disk/by-id and filesystem UUIDs provide more stable references for appropriate tasks.

Before any destructive operation, match the guest device to the hypervisor or hardware inventory using size, serial, model, and relationships. Confirm that it is not a parent of the root filesystem, swap, an encrypted mapping, LVM, RAID, or another active consumer. No single “not mounted” check proves a device is unused.
Linux example — 9.2
List physical and virtual block-device identities.
lsblk -d -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,SERIAL

blocks.text: The tree helps show partitions and device-mapper layers. A blank filesystem column does not prove a device contains nothing valuable; signatures may be absent, unsupported, hidden behind another layer, or damaged.

For scripts, use documented structured output such as --json with explicit columns rather than parsing aligned terminal text. Even structured discovery should not automatically authorize erasure. Human approval or an equally strong provisioning contract must establish that the device is intentionally disposable. (R20)

blocks.text: blkid probes block-device metadata and can report filesystem type, UUID, and label. It complements lsblk by identifying recognized on-disk signatures.
sudo blkid
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: A filesystem UUID identifies the filesystem, not necessarily the underlying physical disk. Reformatting creates a new filesystem identity; cloning can copy an existing UUID and create ambiguity when both copies are attached.

Use direct, appropriately privileged probing when you need current metadata rather than relying on possibly incomplete cached information. After cloning or storage replacement, verify that persistent mount references identify exactly the intended filesystem. A boot failure after a disk change can be an identity problem rather than missing data.
Linux example — 9.4
Read filesystem signatures.
sudo blkid

topics.title: 9.5 Partition Tables
topics.summary: A partition table describes regions of a disk assigned to partitions. It is separate from the filesystems inside those regions. Changing a partition boundary does not automatically transform or resize the filesystem it contains.

blocks.text: A partition table describes regions of a disk assigned to partitions. It is separate from the filesystems inside those regions. Changing a partition boundary does not automatically transform or resize the filesystem it contains.

Preserve the starting sector of an existing filesystem when performing an approved growth operation. Moving the start is a different and much riskier task. Before changes, save the partition layout and ensure the backup is stored somewhere other than the device being modified.

For a new lab disk, plan alignment, boot requirements, data separation, and future growth. For an existing production disk, do not replace the table simply because a tool presents a cleaner-looking layout. The table is a map to existing data, not a cosmetic preference.
Linux example — 9.5
List partition layouts without writing them.
sudo fdisk -l

topics.title: 9.6 GPT and MBR
topics.summary: GPT is the modern partition-table format commonly paired with UEFI systems and supports more flexible partitioning than the older MBR scheme. MBR has historical size and partition-count limitations whose practical effect depends on sector size and layout.

blocks.text: GPT is the modern partition-table format commonly paired with UEFI systems and supports more flexible partitioning than the older MBR scheme. MBR has historical size and partition-count limitations whose practical effect depends on sector size and layout.

GPT includes redundant metadata, but that does not make it a data backup. Corrupting a filesystem or losing the device is still a separate failure. Likewise, a valid partition table does not prove every partition contains a valid filesystem.

Use the format appropriate to the platform and operating-system requirements. Converting a live boot disk between schemes is a planned migration, not a routine command to try during an unrelated outage.

topics.title: 9.8 Creating Filesystems
topics.summary: A filesystem organizes storage into objects, metadata, and allocation structures. mkfs.ext4 and mkfs.xfs create different filesystem formats. They do not preserve the previous contents as a recoverable version.

blocks.text: A filesystem organizes storage into objects, metadata, and allocation structures. mkfs.ext4 and mkfs.xfs create different filesystem formats. They do not preserve the previous contents as a recoverable version.

Before formatting, establish the target identity, required filesystem, label or UUID plan, mount location, capacity, backup status, and approval. Existing signatures are a reason to stop and investigate, not a reason to add a force option automatically.

The worked example formats a newly created ordinary file, then mounts it through a loop device. This is sufficient to learn filesystem creation and mounting. Production devices add additional requirements around alignment, encryption, storage redundancy, support, and recovery.
Linux example — 9.8
Create a filesystem inside a newly created file, not a disk.

lab=$(mktemp -d)
truncate -s 64M "$lab/ext4.img"
mkfs.ext4 -F "$lab/ext4.img"
blkid -p "$lab/ext4.img"
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: -F is used only on this fresh regular-file image; never substitute an existing device.

topics.title: 9.9 ext4
topics.summary: ext4 is a widely used Linux filesystem supporting journaling and established administration tools. Journaling improves recovery of filesystem consistency after some interruptions; it does not guarantee that every application write was durably committed.

blocks.text: ext4 is a widely used Linux filesystem supporting journaling and established administration tools. Journaling improves recovery of filesystem consistency after some interruptions; it does not guarantee that every application write was durably committed.

resize2fs manages ext-family filesystem size under supported conditions. Growth can often occur while mounted; shrinking requires an offline procedure and careful coordination with the underlying device. The exact support depends on the filesystem and kernel environment.

Use e2fsck for appropriate offline checks, not a generic repair command against a busy mounted filesystem. Before any repair, preserve data or an image when possible and investigate underlying storage errors. Repeated repair without fixing failing hardware can worsen data loss. (R21)

blocks.text: XFS is another mature Linux filesystem used commonly in enterprise environments. It supports online growth and has its own tools, including xfs_growfs, xfs_info, and xfs_repair.

For the RHEL 9 teaching baseline, plan XFS capacity changes as grow-only. Do not shrink the underlying logical volume beneath an XFS filesystem. To move to a smaller allocation, create a new appropriately sized filesystem and perform a verified migration or restore.

xfs_growfs normally operates on the mounted filesystem’s mount point. xfs_repair has different requirements and risks from ext4’s repair tools. A familiar-looking filesystem problem does not justify using another filesystem’s repair command. (R22)
Linux example — 9.10
Inspect XFS capabilities without formatting storage.

mkfs.xfs -V
findmnt -t xfs
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: An empty mount listing can simply mean this host has no mounted XFS filesystem.

topics.title: 9.11 Mounting Filesystems
topics.summary: Mounting attaches a filesystem to a directory in the visible tree. The directory must exist, and existing contents beneath it become hidden while the mount is active. A mount can have options governing execution, devices, privilege bits, access mode, and other behavior.

blocks.text: Mounting attaches a filesystem to a directory in the visible tree. The directory must exist, and existing contents beneath it become hidden while the mount is active. A mount can have options governing execution, devices, privilege bits, access mode, and other behavior.

findmnt -T /var
mount | head -n 10
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: Use findmnt for precise inspection rather than parsing an unbounded human-oriented mount listing in automation. Mount options such as nosuid, nodev, and noexec can reduce certain risks, but they are not a complete sandbox.

Unmounting requires that the filesystem no longer be in use under normal conditions. Diagnose users with tools such as fuser or lsof; do not immediately reach for forced or lazy unmounting on a service’s active data path. (R23)
Linux example — 9.11
Mount the section 9.8 image read-only in the lab VM.

mkdir "$lab/mount"
sudo mount -o loop,ro "$lab/ext4.img" "$lab/mount"
findmnt -T "$lab/mount"
sudo umount "$lab/mount"

reading.title: 9.11 Mounting Filesystems
paragraphs: Mounting attaches a filesystem to a directory in the visible tree. The directory must exist, and existing contents beneath it become hidden while the mount is active. A mount can have options governing execution, devices, privilege bits, access mode, and other behavior.

Use findmnt for precise inspection rather than parsing an unbounded human-oriented mount listing in automation. Mount options such as nosuid, nodev, and noexec can reduce certain risks, but they are not a complete sandbox.

Unmounting requires that the filesystem no longer be in use under normal conditions. Diagnose users with tools such as fuser or lsof; do not immediately reach for forced or lazy unmounting on a service’s active data path. (R23)

blocks.text: /etc/fstab describes persistent mounts and swap according to fields for source, target, type, options, dump, and filesystem-check order. On systemd systems, a generator translates relevant entries into units.
A typical data entry might use a filesystem UUID and an explicit mount point. The actual UUID must come from the intended device. Do not copy an example UUID from documentation.

Before applying changes, save a protected copy and use findmnt --verify --verbose to check the table. Run systemctl daemon-reload after changing fstab on a systemd host, then test the specific mount. A successful mount test is stronger than syntax alone. Do not reboot to discover a typo that could have been checked while access still worked.

topics.title: 9.15 Disk Usage

blocks.text: Storage usage can mean allocated blocks, apparent file size, filesystem capacity, snapshots, thin-pool consumption, or underlying provisioned storage. These measurements are related but not identical.

A sparse file can have a large apparent size while using few blocks. A snapshot can retain old blocks no longer visible in the current filesystem view. A deleted-but-open file can consume space without appearing in an ordinary directory scan.

Ask which layer’s capacity is exhausted. A filesystem may have free space while its thin pool is nearly full, or the underlying cloud disk may be large while the filesystem remains small. Monitoring must cover the layers that can independently stop writes.
Linux example — 9.15
Measure your own home directory.

du -sh "$HOME"
df -h "$HOME"

df -h /var

blocks.text: -x keeps the du walk on one filesystem, and -d1 limits displayed depth in GNU du. Even a bounded-depth report can scan many descendants, so consider load on a busy host.

Differences can result from open deleted files, inaccessible paths, reserved blocks, metadata, sparse allocation, snapshots, or mounts hiding underlying files. Do not “correct” the discrepancy by deleting random large directories. Use it as a clue about which objects each tool can see.

topics.title: 9.17 Filesystem Repair
topics.summary: Repair modifies filesystem metadata to recover a usable structure. It can discard damaged information and should not be treated as a harmless diagnostic. Prefer read-only assessment and a recoverable image or backup before destructive repair when feasible.

blocks.text: Repair modifies filesystem metadata to recover a usable structure. It can discard damaged information and should not be treated as a harmless diagnostic. Prefer read-only assessment and a recoverable image or backup before destructive repair when feasible.

Use the filesystem-specific tool and its required mount state. ext4 checks normally use e2fsck on an unmounted filesystem. XFS repair uses xfs_repair on an unmounted filesystem; forcing log destruction is a high-risk last resort with possible data loss, not a default flag.

If storage hardware is failing, repeated scans may increase stress. Escalate to an appropriate recovery procedure and preserve the best available copy. A repaired filesystem also needs application-level validation: directory consistency does not prove a database is logically correct.

topics.summary: Expand from the outside inward: provision more device capacity, extend a partition if used, extend a physical volume if used, allocate logical-volume space if used, and finally grow the filesystem. The exact sequence depends on the actual stack.

blocks.text: Expand from the outside inward: provision more device capacity, extend a partition if used, extend a physical volume if used, allocate logical-volume space if used, and finally grow the filesystem. The exact sequence depends on the actual stack.

After each step, inspect the layer’s reported size before continuing. A command that enlarges a logical volume without growing its filesystem has not yet supplied the application with more file capacity.

Growth still needs a backup and a rollback or recovery plan. “Usually online” is not the same as “risk-free.” Verify application writes, free capacity, persistent mount identity, and behavior after a controlled reboot when the maintenance plan permits it.

labs.title: Detect inode exhaustion independently of bytes
labs.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
lab_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$lab_dir"' EXIT
cd -- "$lab_dir"
printf 'bytes_free=1048576\ninodes_free=0\n' > capacity.fixture
. ./capacity.fixture
test "$bytes_free" -gt 0 && test "$inodes_free" -eq 0
printf 'bytes available; inode boundary exhausted\n'
